# Impact of Four-Day Work Weeks on Software Team Output

## Methods

We conducted a six-month controlled field study across three engineering teams
(N = 47 engineers) at a mid-size software company. One team retained the
standard five-day schedule (control), while two teams adopted a compressed
four-day, 32-hour week (treatment). Assignment to conditions was not randomized;
teams self-selected into the treatment based on manager willingness.

Productivity was operationalized as the number of merged pull requests per
engineer per week, extracted automatically from the version-control system. We
also collected self-reported burnout using a five-item Likert survey
administered monthly. Differences between conditions were tested using a
two-sample t-test on the weekly per-engineer PR counts, with significance set
at p < 0.05. No correction for multiple comparisons was applied.

## Results

Treatment teams merged 11 percent more pull requests per engineer per week than
the control team (p = 0.04). Self-reported burnout fell by 0.6 points on the
five-point scale in treatment teams.

## Conclusion

The four-day week improved throughput without harming perceived well-being.
target_answer: The analysis should extract the study's methodology (a six-month non-randomized controlled field study using PR counts and a Likert burnout survey, analyzed with a two-sample t-test), summarize how field practice typically evaluates such interventions, and flag methodological risks such as the lack of randomization, self-selection bias, small sample, and no correction for multiple comparisons. It should offer concrete suggestions for improvement.

# Lightweight Transformer for On-Device Intent Classification

## Methodology

We fine-tune a 4-layer DistilBERT encoder on a proprietary dataset of 82,000
labeled user utterances spanning 30 intent classes. The data were split
70/15/15 into train, validation, and test sets by random sampling at the
utterance level. Text was lowercased and tokenized with the standard WordPiece
tokenizer; sequences were truncated to 48 tokens.

Training used the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 3e-5, batch size 64,
and early stopping on validation macro-F1 with a patience of three epochs. All
runs were executed on a single A100 GPU. We report macro-F1 and per-class
precision and recall on the held-out test set, averaged over three seeds.

## Results

The model reached a macro-F1 of 0.91 on the test set and ran inference in under
9 ms per utterance on a mobile CPU.
target_answer: The analysis should extract the fine-tuning methodology (DistilBERT on 82k utterances, 70/15/15 split, AdamW, macro-F1 over three seeds) and compare it to standard practice in NLP intent classification. It should note strengths (multiple seeds, held-out test set) and gaps or risks (single dataset, no baseline comparison, no confidence intervals) and suggest improvements.
